Equity research · factor study

How much oil is left in Oslo Børs?

Oil-price sensitivity of 63 Norwegian stocks and 10 sectors, 2007–2026: two-factor betas with confidence intervals, a rule-based event study, scenario tables and an out-of-sample check.

0.29oil beta of the index, full sample
0.13same, latest two-year window
69rule-based oil shocks studied
90%of shocks where past betas ranked stocks correctly

What the data says

  1. The oil beta of Oslo Børs has gone from 0.49 to 0.13. Over the full sample a 10% move in Brent has come with a 2.9% move in the benchmark index. The rolling two-year beta averaged 0.49 up to 2013, 0.21 since 2015, and is 0.13 today.
  2. Only energy carries oil risk beyond the index. Once the index is held fixed, 16 of 63 stocks keep a significantly positive oil beta, 15 of them in E&P and oil service. The most negative partial beta belongs to Norwegian Air Shuttle (-0.32), where fuel is a cost.
  3. Over the last five years oil has stopped mattering for 4 of 10 sectors. For technology & renewables, banks & insurance, seafood, consumer, telecom & real estate the recent total oil beta cannot be told apart from zero. Exploration & production still moves +5.3% for a +10% Brent move.
  4. Oil shocks are priced within two days. Across 69 rule-based shocks the reaction lands in the [0,+1] window. Betas measured only in those shock days line up with ordinary weekly betas (correlation 0.89 across stocks).
  5. Sensitivity is stable, predictability is absent. Betas estimated only on past data rank stocks correctly in the next shock (mean rank correlation +0.28, t = 10.5, positive in 90% of shocks). The same ranking says nothing about the following days (-0.01, t = -0.3). This is a risk tool, not a trading signal.
  6. The downside beta is larger. The index's oil beta is 0.37 in weeks when oil falls and 0.19 when it rises (p = 0.012). Large oil declines tend to be demand scares that hit all equities, so part of this is shared macro news rather than oil itself.
Step 1

A data foundation that can be audited

Prices are auto-adjusted closes from Yahoo Finance, pinned to a fixed end date (2026-09-11) and described in data/manifest.json. Three rules separate this from a typical correlation study:

  • Align first, then compute returns. Brent trades on days Oslo is closed. Returns are taken on the common calendar (4,610 days), so a holiday is folded into the next return instead of pairing mismatched periods.
  • No double counting. Sector series are equal-weighted portfolios of their members. No index or ETF is averaged with its own constituents.
  • Weekly returns for betas. Oslo closes about six hours before Brent settles; Friday-to-Friday returns dilute that timing gap and the stale prices of small caps.

The benchmark is OSEBX, chained with OSEFX returns before 2013-03-05 because Yahoo's OSEBX history starts there. In the 625-day overlap the two have a return correlation of 0.990.

Manual interventions (all of them)

  • AKSO.OL 2024-11-25: Extraordinary dividend (~NOK 21/share) missing from Yahoo's adjustment: a -41% print that was really a cash payout
  • SOFF.OL 2020-10-21: Restructuring / share consolidation mis-adjusted by Yahoo (-98% print)
  • BORR.OL 2021-12-13: 2:1 reverse split applied one day late by Yahoo (price doubles, then reverts)
  • BORR.OL 2021-12-14: Second leg of the same split artefact
  • NEL.OL from 2014-10-01: Listed shell was DiaGenic (diagnostics) until it bought NEL Hydrogen in Oct 2014

Still flagged but kept, because the moves are real or the issue is mild: DNO (extreme print); Borr Drilling (extreme print); Frontline (extreme print); MPC Container Ships (extreme print); Grieg Seafood (extreme print); Norwegian Air Shuttle (extreme print); Bouvet (stale prices).

Step 2

Two oil betas, because there are two questions

r = α + βmkt·MARKET + βoil·BRENT + ε on weekly log returns, Newey-West standard errors.
Partial beta: the index enters as it is — oil exposure beyond what the index already carries. Total beta: the index is first stripped of its own oil component — what happens to the stock when Brent moves, through every channel. Identity: total = partial + βmkt × (the index's own oil beta).
Step 3

Event study: what happens when oil jumps

A shock is any day where the Brent return exceeds 2.5 trailing standard deviations (volatility measured up to the day before). Shocks within 11 trading days of an accepted one are skipped, leaving 69 events (22 up, 47 down). Abnormal returns use a market model fitted on days -270 to -21.

Step 5

Regimes

Splitting by trailing oil volatility instead (above or below its expanding median, known before the week starts) changes little: the index's beta is 0.27 in calm and 0.22 in turbulent periods (p = 0.25). The regime that matters is direction, not volatility.

Step 6

Side analysis: is there an oil factor in the returns themselves?

PC1 is the market. PC2 separates seafood from energy and has a 0.28 correlation with Brent: returns alone do not single out oil as the second driver of Oslo Børs.

All stocks

What this study cannot tell you

  • Survivorship. The universe is today's listings with Yahoo history. Names that have left Yahoo's Oslo feed (PGS, Seadrill, Golden Ocean, Flex LNG) are missing, so the sample is tilted towards survivors.
  • Correlation with a sign, not causation. Brent moves for demand and supply reasons. A demand scare moves oil and equities together without oil causing anything.
  • Equal weights, hand-made sectors. Sector portfolios are not investable indices; Equinor counts as much as Panoro.
  • USD oil, NOK stocks. The krone's own oil sensitivity is part of the total beta by design and is not separated out.
  • Vendor data. Yahoo adjustments contain errors; every one found is listed above, others may remain.
